headline: Parliament confirms Mehrdad Akhlaqi Ketabchi as defence minister (237/277 votes), first remarks warn of 'surprising and'
dek: Iran's parliament approved Mehrdad Akhlaqi Ketabchi as defence and armed-forces logistics minister with 237 votes in favour, 15 against (277 cast), in a video-conference session. He replaces Majid Ebn al-Reza (acting) and Aziz Nasirzadeh, killed in the initial US-Israeli attacks on Feb 28.
sources: Iranian state television / ISNA; Reuters Newsroom; AA; Straits Times/AFP; JPost
fault_line: Will Akhlaqi rebuild Iran's military command — or share his predecessors' fate?

sections.what_happened: Iran's parliament has confirmed Mehrdad Akhlaqi Ketabchi as defence and armed-forces logistics minister, with two hundred thirty-seven votes in favour and fifteen against, out of two hundred seventy-seven cast, in a video-conference session. The veteran has spent forty-two years inside the defence ministry and has headed the Defence Industries Organisation since twenty thirteen. He replaces Majid Ebn al-Reza, who had been serving in an acting capacity, and formally succeeds Aziz Nasirzadeh, the defence minister killed in the opening hours of the United States-Israeli attacks on February twenty-eighth. In his first remarks, Akhlaqi warned that any new American or Israeli attack would draw what he called a surprising and extensive response, and said a new strike would cost American lives.
sections.what_verified: The vote count and the quotes are confirmed across the board: Reuters, AFP, the Anadolu Agency, NDTV and the Economic Times all report the same numbers, and even the Jerusalem Post confirms them. There are no contradictions between wire and regional outlets on the basic facts. Akhlaqi's biography — four decades in the ministry, head of the Defence Industries Organisation since twenty thirteen — is a matter of public record, as is the fact that he carries United Nations sanctions from his time running the missile-industry apparatus. Nasirzadeh's death in the February twenty-eighth strikes is established.
sections.what_disputed: The minister's claim that Iran now possesses countermeasures against the American MOAB-class bunker-buster munitions is a primary-source claim — it comes from the minister himself, and no independent source has verified it. Western outlets are framing Akhlaqi primarily through his sanctions record, presenting the missile-industry veteran as a hardliner rather than engaging with the substance of his warning. Whether his 'surprising and extensive' threat reflects real new capabilities or deterrence theatre is not independently checkable from open sources.
sections.why_matters: Eight months after its defence minister was killed on day one of the war, Iran has ended the interim arrangement and put the missile industry's own chief in charge of the armed forces' logistics. That is not the move of a military in collapse; it is the move of a state rebuilding its command around the one industrial base — missiles and drones — that has defined the entire war. The appointment also tells Washington and Tel Aviv exactly who they would be striking next: the man who built the arsenal they failed to destroy in February.
sections.context: The Defence Industries Organisation that Akhlaqi ran for over a decade is the backbone of Iran's missile and drone production — the same arsenal that has sustained the pressure campaign across the region through eight months of war. His predecessor Nasirzadeh was killed in the first wave of the February twenty-eighth attacks, which were presented in Western capitals as a decapitation of Iran's military leadership. The fact that his successor is the missile industry's chief, confirmed by an overwhelming parliamentary majority, suggests the decapitation narrative did not survive contact with Iran's institutional depth.

totw_analysis: The Western telling of this story writes itself: sanctioned missile chief takes over a broken military. Read it from Tehran's side and the picture inverts. In February, the United States and Israel opened the war by killing Iran's defence minister in his office. Eight months later, Iran's answer is to promote the man who ran the missile factories — confirmed by two hundred thirty-seven votes to fifteen, in a parliament that does not hand out those margins lightly. That is a state advertising continuity, not scrambling. The 'surprising and extensive' warning is doing two jobs at once: it tells the Iranian public the command is whole, and it tells Washington that the February playbook — kill the leadership, collapse the system — has a named, living rebuttal. On the MOAB-countermeasure claim, honesty requires the label: this is the minister talking about his own arsenal, and no outside source can confirm it. But note what the Western framing leaves out. Nobody in Washington or Tel Aviv is disputing that the missiles kept coming for eight months after they killed the last minister. Akhlaqi does not need to prove his countermeasures work. He only needs the next American planner to wonder whether they do. Deterrence is not about certainty. It is about the doubt you plant in the other side's targeting meeting. That is the whole appointment, in one sentence.
